newsitem.title: BRAZIL: U.S. shows South America how to fight drugs money.
newsitem.headline: U.S. shows South America how to fight drugs money.

text.p: South American tax officials gathered in the Brazilian capital on Monday to hear from the United States how it could help stem a multibillion-dollar flow of drug money in the region.

"Money-laundering is now a worldwide problem ... and needs the work of all of us," Thomas Brown, head of narcotics and money laundering with the United States Internal Revenue Service (IRS), said at the opening of an international seminar on the subject.

Every year, an estimated $1.5 trillion in cash made worldwide from drugs, illegal arms sales, corruption and organized crime switches from account to account, often crossing several borders, before ending up as apparently legitimate funds.

The U.S. government has said it would consider trade and other sanctions against countries who repeatedly refuse to introduce laws against money-laundering, just as it has decertified Colombia for failing to do enough to halt the drugs trade.

In Brazil, which has strict banking secrecy laws, sophisticated financial markets and a steady flow of cocaine from neighboring Andean nations, officials say $30 billion has been laundered since 1990, making it one of the world's top 10 money-laundering nations.

"Our bank secrecy laws are considered sacred ... but have covered up fraud, smuggling and tax evasion. In brief, they are a shelter for crime," Everardo Maciel, the head of Brazil's Internal Revenue Service, said.

A bill giving tax investigators greater powers to delve into suspect accounts is currently awaiting approval in Brazil's Congress. Officials probing the latest corruption scandal involving public funds say the bill is needed urgently.
"We need that legislation approved now," Maciel said.

Brazil and the United States are due to begin negotiating an accord to share data on tax investigations. Money-laundering is likely to be one of the main topics on President Bill Clinton's agenda when he visits the region in May.

But officials conceded that organized crime was always likely to find alternative ways of cleansing their ill-gotten fortunes. "We know we've been successful when our cases suddenly dry up," said Brown of the IRS.

Despite the United States' efforts to bring Latin America's lawmakers up to speed, "a tremendous amount of money-laundering is done inside our borders ... which nevers goes to other countries," he said.
